messages.subject: Question about fitting models without dynamic error in dynr
messages.subject_clean: Question about fitting models without dynamic error in dynr
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sir, Madam, or to whom this may concern,

my name is Jan Failenschmid and I am part of a research group at Tilburg University. As part of our project "Nonlinear Methods for Intensive Longitudinal Data" we are exploring how well different non-linear processes can be described by a variety of parametric and non-parametric methods. To this end, we intend to compare different conditions in a simulation study such as:  linear vs. continuous and differentiable non-linear trends, smooth vs. catastrophic change, and stochastic vs. deterministic state equations.

To us, dynr has been perfect for modelling the more complex processes that arise from these conditions. However, since we would like to keep the modelling frameworks in our project consistent, we were wondering whether dynr is also able to fit the simple models without any regime-switching and without dynamic error. For example, we would like to include a simple linear trend model as a baseline and comparison model (of the sort that could be fit using the lm() function), which seems in theory possible by estimating the intercept as the
initial state value of the state space model and adding the slope at each time step in the state equation.

Judging from the tutorials on your website and other documentation, this practice seems to deviate from the intended purpose of the package, and we therefore wanted to ask you about whether this is sensible to do or whether you would recommend using different functions for these simpler models. Especially, since dynr's optimizer ran into a lot of numeric underflow issues, while testing models without dynamic errors, that we had to counteract by starting the optimizer with very large initial values for the measurement variance. Additionally, we were worrying about the asymptotic efficiency of the state-space model based estimation procedure in dynr relative to simpler estimation procedures, for these simpler models and wanted to ask whether you have any resources about this.

If it would be helpful for you, we have examples of the models in question and working code that we could send you.

Thank you very much for your time and tremendous help in advance.

Kind regards,

Jan Failenschmid

messages.subject_clean: Question about fitting models without dynamic error in dynr
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan!

Thanks for using dynr!  I'm glad it's been the right tool for some of your modeling tasks.

In general, dynr is able to fit models without regime-swtiching and without dynamic error.  For non-regime-switching models, just specify a single regime in dynr.model() and in the corresponding "recipes": prep.measurement(), prep.initial(), prep.noise(), prep.linearDynamics()/prep.formulaDynamics(), etc.  For models without dynamic error, just specify prep.noise() with values.latent and params.latent indicating zero variance and fixed values.  Internally and for numerical stability, dynr changes zero variances to a small positive value: 1x10^-6, if memory serves.

There are several ways to fit simple linear trends.  The approach you outlined of having a recursive accumulation at a constant rate is one possibility.  Another is to fully specify a linear latent growth curve model.  Although using OpenMx instead of dynr, this paper (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2017.1369354) shows on page 319 under the heading "Multiple Subjects Latent Growth" how to write a linear latent growth curve as a state space model.  The dynr package can fit the same model.

As you note, the optimization in dynr can be a bit sensitive.  I've had the most success in dealing with this by using bounds on free parameters.  This script (https://github.com/mhunter1/dynr/blob/master/inst/models/passing/LinearSDEWithChecks.R#L87) shows how to set upper bounds (ub) and lower bounds (lb).

I hope this helps you on the right track.  Feel free to reach out again!

Cheers,
Mike Hunter
Developer/Maintainer of dynr
Assistant Professor of Human Development and Family Studies
Pennsylvania State University
